tldr: By applying the local learning rule e-prop to a 3D spiking neural network (SNN) that mimics cultured neural circuits and distilling a reinforcement learning policy, researchers achieved a 100% survival rate in simulated locomotion of the full-size humanoid H1-2, along with several seconds of bipedal stepping on the physical robot.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed closed-loop control system. Using DAgger with output labels from a reinforcement learning expert, a 3D SNN model of 512 neurons is trained to control the full-size humanoid H1-2 through PD controllers.
overview:
In recent years, wetware computing using biological brain organoids and cultured neurons has attracted growing interest. However, whether such biological neural circuits can control a full-size humanoid robot requiring continuous whole-body balance has remained an open question.

In this study, the authors developed an SNN model of 512 Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons that faithfully replicates the dynamics and connectivity of neural tissue cultured in 3D around microbeads on a microelectrode array (MEA). Using an imitation learning framework to distill a walking expert policy pretrained with reinforcement learning, they compared four learning schemes with different levels of biological plausibility: a fixed reservoir, three-factor reward-modulated STDP, the local learning rule e-prop, and non-biological backpropagation through time (BPTT).

In MuJoCo physics simulations, e-prop—which pairs local eligibility traces with neuron-specific error signals—achieved a 100% survival rate (completing full 10-second episodes), matching BPTT, which backpropagates full gradients backward through time. In contrast, schemes commonly envisioned for biological cultures plateaued at much lower performance: ~43.7% for the fixed reservoir and ~11.2% for uniform reward-modulated STDP. When transferred zero-shot to the physical Unitree H1-2, the robot demonstrated sustained bipedal stepping for 3 to 9 seconds before eventually falling due to modeling discrepancies.
contributions: Constructed an SNN model that faithfully mirrors the geometry and electrophysiological parameters of an in-vitro 3D neural tissue culture.
Demonstrated that e-prop, a biologically plausible local learning rule, matches non-biological BPTT with a 100% survival rate in humanoid walking simulations.
Identified why fixed reservoirs and global reward-modulated STDP fail, revealing the vital importance of neuron-specific 'addressed feedback' to synapses.
Demonstrated several seconds of closed-loop bipedal stepping on the full-size physical humanoid H1-2 using an SNN trained with a biologically plausible local rule.

sections.heading: Can Cultured Brain Tissue Walk a Humanoid?
sections.summary: As computing with cultured biological neurons gains traction, this paper asks whether an SNN mimicking in-vitro neural circuits can achieve closed-loop balance control of a full-size humanoid using biologically plausible learning rules. Comparing four methods across biological plausibility levels reveals the decisive factors for performance.
sections.details:
In modern humanoid robotics, deep reinforcement learning (DeepRL) trained on massive parallel GPU setups has become the de facto standard for locomotion. In parallel, researchers have explored wetware computation, using biological neural cultures or brain organoids for tasks like speech recognition and nonlinear equation forecasting via reservoir computing.

However, real biological cultures suffer from poor repeatability across preparations and require substantial time to grow. To bridge this gap, the authors drew inspiration from '3D neural tissue assemblies' grown around microbeads. Replicating this biologically faithful 3D tissue architecture in simulation, they addressed a fundamental question: can a network trained with biologically plausible rules walk a full-size humanoid without falling?

This study compares four learning schemes within the exact same control pipeline, ordered from most to least biologically plausible:
- Fixed reservoir (frozen recurrent weights, training only a linear readout)
- Three-factor reward-modulated STDP (dopamine-like learning driven by a global scalar reward)
- Eligibility propagation / e-prop (a local forward approximation of BPTT using local traces and neuron-specific feedback)
- BPTT (a non-biological theoretical baseline backpropagating loss gradients through time)

By distilling an RL expert policy into these networks, the paper explores whether biological realism and high-performance robotic control can go hand in hand.

captions.P1: The closed-loop control pipeline. The 512-neuron 3D SNN receives a 45-dimensional observation vector and outputs 12-DoF target joint positions, which drive the H1-2 robot in MuJoCo via 1 kHz PD controllers.

sections.heading: At the Crossroads of Humanoid Locomotion, Neuromorphic Control, and Cultured Tissue
sections.summary: This section reviews reinforcement learning for locomotion, motor control with spiking neural networks (SNNs), and computational modeling of 3D biological neural cultures. The paper unites these fields to attempt full-size humanoid walking powered by biologically plausible local learning.
sections.details:
### Humanoid Locomotion and Expert Policies
State-of-the-art humanoid locomotion relies heavily on model predictive control (MPC) and parallelized RL. In this work, the SNN learns from a 'Constraints as Terminations (CaT)' RL expert policy. The objective is not to outperform the expert, but to see if its robust locomotion can be reproduced under biological learning constraints.

### Neuromorphic Locomotion Control
Prior work has explored central pattern generators (CPGs) and simulated arm-leg coordination using SNNs. However, these networks were not constrained by the physical geometry or connectivity rules of real cultured tissue, nor did they maintain closed-loop balance on a full-size physical humanoid.

### 3D Neural Tissue Assemblies and Reservoir Computing
Using in-vitro networks grown on microelectrode arrays as computational reservoirs is an appealing strategy because it avoids internal credit assignment. This study directly adopts the geometric dimensions and connectivity rules of previously established 3D cultured microelectrode platforms.

### SNN Learning Rules
Because spikes are non-differentiable, BPTT with surrogate gradients is commonly applied. However, BPTT transmits errors backward through time, which is biologically impossible. The authors look to more biologically plausible alternatives: global reward-modulated STDP and e-prop, which computes gradient approximations forward in time.

sections.heading: Designing the Robot Environment and I/O Interface
sections.summary: The experimental platform is the 27-DoF full-size humanoid Unitree H1-2, actuated across the 12 degrees of freedom required for walking at a 50 Hz control rate. The closed-loop setup maps 45-dimensional observations to target joint positions fed into PD controllers.
sections.details:
### Robot and Simulation Environment
The target robot is the Unitree H1-2, a full-size humanoid measuring roughly 1.8 m tall with 27 degrees of freedom. This study controls 12 degrees of freedom concentrated in the lower body. The expert policy was pretrained using PPO for about $3 \times 10^8$ steps across 4096 parallel Isaac Lab environments, then run in MuJoCo to gather dataset trajectories. The control loop runs at 50 Hz (20 ms).

### PD Control and Actuation
Torque $\tau$ for each actuated joint follows standard PD control:
$$\tau = k_p (q_{\mathrm{ref}} - q) + k_d (\dot{q}_{\mathrm{ref}} - \dot{q})$$
Here, $q_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the target joint angle generated by the SNN, while $q$ and $\dot{q}$ are measured states. The target joint velocity $\dot{q}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is set to 0, meaning the D-gain acts purely as damping against joint motion.

### Observation and Action Spaces
- Observation space (45 dimensions): base link angular velocity (3), projected gravity vector (3), velocity commands (3), joint position errors relative to the default standing pose (12), joint velocity errors (12), and the previous action (12).
- Action space (12 dimensions): target joint position offsets for the 12 joints. These are scaled by $c_a = 0.25$ and added to the default standing posture.

sections.heading: A 3D SNN Modeled After Microbead-Stacked Neural Cultures
sections.summary: Based on in-vitro experiments, the network places 512 LIF neurons across a 4-layer 3D grid. It incorporates realistic physiological mechanisms such as Dale's principle and short-term synaptic plasticity (STP).
sections.details:
### Neuron Model
Built upon the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) model—where membrane potential $v$ fires and resets upon crossing threshold $V_{\mathrm{th}}$—the network adds a spike-frequency adaptation (SFA) current $I^a$ to suppress runaway firing. Membrane time constants $\tau_m$ are distributed log-uniformly between 20 and 300 ms to provide biological heterogeneity. The absolute refractory period is 2 ms.

### 3D Network Geometry and Connectivity
Neurons are distributed across a 4-layer grid resembling stacked 45 $\mu$m microbeads on MEA electrodes, with an intra-layer density of 1000 cells/$\mathrm{mm}^2$. The network contains 512 neurons (80% excitatory: 410; 20% inhibitory: 102). Connection probabilities follow a 3D Gaussian distribution based on Euclidean distance, set higher within the same layer ($p_{\max} = 0.20$) than across layers ($p_{\max} = 0.0667$). This yields a sparse overall connectivity of ~6.0%. Dale's principle is strictly enforced: excitatory neurons only possess positive weights, and inhibitory neurons only negative weights.

### Synaptic Dynamics and Short-Term Plasticity (STP)
The Tsodyks-Markram model simulates neurotransmitter release probability (facilitation) and resource availability (depression). Parameters are configured so that depression with a time constant of $\tau_r = 500$ ms dominates, preventing runaway burst activity.

### Readout Layer
Spike trains from the 512 neurons are filtered with an exponential smoothing filter (time constant $\tau_{\mathrm{out}} = 20$ ms) and mapped to 12-dimensional continuous commands via weight matrix $W^{\mathrm{out}}$. This action output is fed back into the next step's observation vector, ensuring the network acts as an active closed-loop controller rather than a passive decoder.

sections.heading: Four Learning Approaches Spanning the Plausibility Spectrum
sections.summary: Sharing an imitation learning baseline (DAgger) to distill the expert, the authors evaluated four schemes that differ in how recurrent synapses are updated: fixed reservoir, 3-factor STDP, e-prop, and BPTT. Local forward dynamics can approximate time-reversed gradients with surprising precision.
sections.details:
### Imitation Learning and the DAgger Framework
Training begins with behavioral cloning (BC) over 50 expert episodes. However, BC alone suffers from covariate shift: small errors compound, leading the robot into unvisited states where it falls. To resolve this, DAgger is executed for 14 rounds, aggregating newly visited states and iteratively retraining.

### Three-Factor Reward-Modulated STDP
This scheme is closest to biological plasticity. Synapses track an eligibility trace $c_{ji}[t]$ based on pre- and post-synaptic spike timing. This trace is modulated by a global scalar neuromodulatory signal (reward $m[t]$) to update weights. However, because every synapse receives the same 1D broadcast, the network cannot determine which specific neuron caused a success or a failure.

### BPTT (Non-Biological Baseline)
BPTT calculates exact loss gradients backward through time over 5000 substeps, differentiating spikes with a surrogate gradient: $\psi_j[t] = 0.6 \max(0, 1 - |v_j[t] - V_{\mathrm{th}}|)$. This provides a theoretical ceiling for performance.

### Eligibility Propagation (e-prop)
In the BPTT computational graph, e-prop drops the backward paths flowing through other neurons (the off-diagonal blocks of the Jacobian) and keeps only each neuron's self-recurrent history. This reduces the update to a purely forward-in-time local rule. Each synapse maintains an eligibility trace $\bar{e}_{ji}[t]$ locally and scales it by an addressed learning signal $L_j[t]$ routed directly from the readout error, approximating BPTT with remarkable fidelity without traveling back in time.

captions.P2: Conceptual diagram of the evaluated learning approaches. It highlights the differences between the fixed reservoir (frozen weights), three-factor STDP (broadcasting a uniform global scalar), and e-prop (multiplying local eligibility traces by neuron-specific feedback signals).

sections.heading: 100% Simulation Survival and Tests on the Real Robot
sections.summary: In MuJoCo simulations, e-prop achieved a 100% survival rate matching BPTT, whereas the fixed reservoir and 3-factor STDP struggled severely. When deployed on the physical H1-2 robot, the network sustained several seconds of bipedal walking steps, highlighting both existing hurdles and real promise.
sections.details:
### Simulation Evaluation: Remarkable Success with Local Learning
All schemes were tested under identical architectures, initializations, and optimizers. Survival rate was measured as the percentage of 10-second episodes completed without falling (base height remaining above 0.5 m).
- Fixed reservoir: Even with DAgger, survival plateaued at $43.7 \pm 4.4$\% due to the limited capacity of its frozen feature space.
- Three-factor STDP: Survival dropped to just $11.2 \pm 1.8$\%, and the average firing rate exploded to 158.1 Hz (63% of the theoretical maximum). A single global reward signal fails at credit assignment.
- e-prop: Achieved a $100.0 \pm 0.0$\% survival rate, matching BPTT ($98.0 \pm 3.0$\%); the average firing rate settled at 10.0 Hz, well within the physiological range of cultured tissue (under ~190 Hz).

Gradient alignment showed a cosine similarity of 0.99 between e-prop update directions and true BPTT gradients, confirming that forward local computations capture the true gradient.

### Deployment on the Physical Unitree H1-2
The e-prop policy trained in simulation was deployed directly onto the real H1-2 robot zero-shot, without domain randomization.
- Seed 1: Walked for 3 seconds before falling.
- Seed 3: Walked for 4 seconds before falling.
- Seed 2: Maintained clear bipedal walking steps for 5 to 9 seconds across 3 consecutive trials.

Although every trial eventually concluded in a fall, the non-biological BPTT policy also fell after a few seconds. This indicates that the failure stems from the Sim-to-Real gap in contact and actuator dynamics, not from shortcomings in the biological learning rule.

captions.P7: (a) Imitation loss progression during behavioral cloning, (b) survival rate improvements across DAgger rounds, and open-loop joint angle tracking with the trained e-prop policy ($R^2 = 0.90$). e-prop cleanly reproduces the expert's periodic walking gait.

sections.heading: A Stepping Stone Toward Biomorphic Wetware Robotics
sections.summary: This study offers the first proof that an SNN faithfully modeling cultured neural tissue can walk a full-size humanoid using biologically plausible learning rules. The linchpin of success was neuron-specific error feedback, providing a crucial design principle for future interfaces with living neural tissue.
sections.details:
In conclusion, the paper demonstrated that an SNN modeled after a 3D neural assembly can maintain fall-free balance locomotion in a simulated full-size humanoid and execute several seconds of stepping on physical hardware.

The key takeaway from the comparative experiments is that 'addressed feedback'—error signals targeted specifically to individual neurons—is essential for biological circuits to master complex motor control. Diffuse global reward broadcasts (R-STDP) and linear readouts over fixed circuits (reservoirs) cannot support high-dimensional dynamic balance.

Looking ahead, closing the Sim-to-Real gap with domain randomization and improving velocity tracking are important next steps. The ultimate research frontier, however, lies in figuring out how to deliver this addressed feedback physically through electrical stimulation to real 3D biological cultures on MEAs.

takeaways: Biologically plausible local learning rules (e-prop) can achieve a 100% survival rate on high-dimensional continuous humanoid control, matching BPTT without backpropagating through time.
Reservoir computing (frozen recurrent weights) and global reward-modulated STDP break down easily; neuron-specific addressed feedback signals are crucial for learning.
An exceptionally lightweight, sparse SNN modeling biological cultured tissue (512 neurons, ~10 Hz average firing) has the representational capacity to control a full-size humanoid.
Sim-to-Real falls were primarily caused by simulator-to-hardware discrepancies in contact and actuator dynamics, rather than limitations inherent to the SNN.
limitations: Despite 100% survival in simulation, the physical H1-2 robot walked for a maximum of 9 seconds before falling in every trial due to the Sim-to-Real gap.
Velocity tracking error was relatively high ($0.71 \text{ m/s}$ compared to the expert's $0.09 \text{ m/s}$), as the policy prioritized balance recovery over speed accuracy.
How to physically implement and deliver the neuron-specific 'addressed feedback' required by e-prop onto real in-vitro biological cultures on microelectrode arrays remains an unsolved challenge.
